screens.title: What is a NavMesh?
screens.narratorSegment: A NavMesh is a precomputed representation of the walkable areas in your scene, expressed as a connected network of polygons. This representation reduces complex geometry to a graph-like surface where each polygon is a region an agent can stand on and pathfinding algorithms compute shortest valid routes between points on that surface. The practical benefit is performance and reliability: path calculations run quickly because they operate on simplified polygons instead of raw mesh triangles, and agents avoid static obstacles automatically because the baking process excludes those areas. For example, imagine a game level with furniture, pillars, and ramps: the NavMesh will create a continuous set of navigable polygons over the floor and ramps while excluding the volume occupied by obstacles, so an enemy can compute a path around a table without per-frame collision checks. A common misconception is that NavMesh replaces physics-based avoidance; it does not. NavMesh handles static and baked geometry and gives agents passable routes, while dynamic obstacle avoidance and steering are still handled by the NavMeshAgent at runtime. Key takeaway: treat the NavMesh as the map of where agents may plan paths, and use agent settings to ensure that map matches your characters' footprint. How does your level geometry change when you imagine different agent sizes?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A NavMesh is a simplified map of walkable polygons generated from scene geometry that AI agents use to compute efficient paths.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.3 › What is a NavMesh?
Definition

A collection of connected polygons representing walkable surfaces. The NavMesh replaces detailed collision geometry for planning and produces a graph agents use for pathfinding.

Bullets
  • Speeds up path calculation by working on polygons rather than mesh triangles.
  • Automatically excludes obstacles so agents route around them.
  • Depends on baking parameters and object settings for accuracy.
Example

A level with pillars: the NavMesh will leave holes where pillars stand so an agent navigates around them without per-frame collision checking.

Key Takeaway

NavMesh is the precomputed map agents use for planning; tune baking to match agent footprint for accurate paths.

Analogy
Think of it as a city sidewalk map: streets and sidewalks are kept, buildings are removed, so routing becomes a simple search across passable polygons.

screens.title: Baking a NavMesh in Unity
screens.narratorSegment: Baking transforms your scene into a NavMesh by scanning geometry and classifying surfaces as walkable or not. Start by opening the Navigation window and switching to the Bake tab. The key parameters there control how the NavMesh is generated: Agent Radius sets the minimum clearance around the agent footprint and influences which narrow passages remain walkable. Agent Height excludes low ceilings where an agent cannot fit. Max Slope limits how steep a surface may be to remain walkable, and Step Height defines the climbable step size. Drop Height and Jump Distance determine how much vertical movement or gaps an agent can traverse during baking. A concrete example: if you set Agent Radius to 0.5 meters and your doorway is 0.8 meters wide, that doorway will be considered passable. If you increase radius to 0.6, the doorway may become unwalkable and the NavMesh will not include it. Important debugging step: mark your ground as Navigation Static and obstacles as Not Walkable before baking; otherwise the NavMesh may include geometry you intend to block. After adjusting parameters, click Bake and inspect the blue overlay in the Scene view. If areas are missing, iteratively adjust parameters rather than assuming an agent bug. Which parameter would you change first if agents cannot climb a ramp? Max Slope is usually the answer.

keyIdea.text: Bake parameters (radius, height, slope, step) determine which areas are walkable; small changes can open or close narrow passages.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.3 › Baking a NavMesh
Key Bake Parameters
Agent Radius
Defines the agent’s clearance; affects narrow passages.
Agent Height
Minimum agent height to detect ceilings and low obstacles.
Max Slope
Highest climbable angle included as walkable.
Step Height
Maximum vertical step the agent can step over during navigation.
Bake checklist
  • Mark ground as Navigation Static (Walkable).
  • Mark obstacles as Navigation Static (Not Walkable).
  • Adjust parameters and click Bake; inspect the resulting overlay.
Example

Doorway width 0.8m: agent radius 0.5m allows passage. If agents get stuck at the doorway, try reducing radius instead of changing runtime steering first.

Visualization
Inspect the blue overlay to ensure walkable areas match your intended level flow. If not, adjust bake parameters and re-bake.

screens.title: Marking Objects for Baking
screens.narratorSegment: The NavMesh only reflects objects you mark for inclusion in baking. In the Inspector, use the Navigation Static dropdown to mark ground and obstacles appropriately. Ground objects you want agents to walk on should be marked as Navigation Static and set to Walkable. Objects that should block navigation—walls, crates, and tall props—should be marked as Navigation Static but flagged Not Walkable, or handled as NavMeshObstacles when runtime movement is required. A common error is forgetting to mark an object as Navigation Static; the bake will then ignore it and agents might attempt to walk through it because it wasn't excluded. Another practical distinction is between static obstacles baked into the NavMesh and dynamic obstacles created at runtime with NavMeshObstacle; the former alters the baked polygons, the latter is resolved by the agent's avoidance system and local steering. For example, if you place a table and forget to mark it Not Walkable, the NavMesh will cover the table top area if it's flagged as walkable, creating a hole in behavior. Best practice: maintain a short checklist—mark ground walkable, mark level architecture as static, and treat moving platforms or doors as dynamic obstacles or update the NavMesh at runtime if necessary. Ask yourself: did I mark every major prop that should block movement as static before baking?

keyIdea.text: Correctly marking objects as Navigation Static and choosing walkable vs not-walkable determines whether the NavMesh will include or exclude them during baking.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.3 › Marking Objects for Baking
Walkable vs Not Walkable

Walkable objects become part of the surface the NavMesh will consider; Not Walkable objects exclude areas and create navigation barriers.

Practical checklist
  • Ground: Navigation Static = Walkable.
  • Walls, fixed obstacles: Navigation Static = Not Walkable.
  • Moving doors or objects: use NavMeshObstacle or update the NavMesh at runtime.
Common Mistake

Not marking a blocking object as Navigation Static can leave holes in navigation or let agents walk through geometry.

Example scenario
You place a large crate as an obstacle. If the crate is not set to Navigation Static Not Walkable, the bake may still mark that area as walkable and agents will attempt to travel through it. Set it correctly then rebake to ensure the obstacle is respected.
Key Takeaway

Mark objects intentionally before baking. Static architecture belongs in the bake; dynamic objects should use runtime avoidance or NavMeshObstacle where appropriate.

screens.title: Agent Parameters and Their Effects
screens.narratorSegment: Agent parameters determine how baking interprets the environment and how agents behave at runtime. Agent Radius is the horizontal clearance the NavMesh assumes an agent needs; larger radii close narrow spaces during baking, while smaller radii can let agents squeeze through tight corridors. Agent Height matters for low ceilings and tunnels—if your character is tall but Agent Height is set low, you may bake walkable areas that real agents cannot occupy. Max Slope controls ramp traversability: set it too low and ramps will be excluded, too high and agents may attempt to climb surfaces you intended as walls. Step Height allows small vertical steps; if it's smaller than curb heights in your level, agents will treat those curbs as obstacles. Contrast two common scenarios: a nimble small enemy versus a large armored boss. You would bake the level with different Agent Radius and Height so both can navigate appropriate routes, or provide separate NavMesh areas per size. A common misconception is that a single NavMesh fits all agent sizes; in practice you may need multiple NavMesh layers or adjust baking for the primary agent type. Which property would you tune first if agents can’t traverse a ramp? Max Slope is the likely candidate, followed by visual confirmation in the Scene view.

Module 06 › Chapter 6.3 › Agent Parameters
Agent Radius
Controls clearance. Larger radius closes narrow paths during baking.
Agent Height
Used to detect ceilings and determine if an agent fits under obstacles.
Max Slope
Highest angle allowed for walkable surfaces.
Step Height
Maximum step the agent can walk over without requiring a ramp.
Scenario comparison

Use smaller radius and height so it can pass through tighter spaces and under low obstacles.
Large boss
Bake with larger radius to prevent it from squeezing through tight corridors you don’t want it to use.

screens.title: NavMeshAgent: The Runtime Bridge
screens.narratorSegment: The NavMeshAgent component is the runtime bridge between your gameplay logic and the precomputed NavMesh. It handles path calculation, steering, and local obstacle avoidance so your scripts can issue simple commands like SetDestination and rely on the agent to move sensibly. When you call SetDestination with a position on the NavMesh, the agent computes a path across polygons and begins moving, steering around static obstacles baked into the NavMesh and responding to dynamic obstacles based on its avoidance settings. For example, in a chase scenario you might increase agent. speed and leave stoppingDistance set to a value greater than zero so the agent approaches the player but does not collide. A frequent misconception is thinking SetDestination teleports or deterministically snaps an agent to the goal; instead it starts a calculated path and the agent follows it over time, subject to speed, acceleration and angular speed. Understanding NavMeshAgent state is important: agent. remainingDistance tells you how far remains on the current path, agent. pathPending indicates if path computation is ongoing, and agent. isStopped can pause movement without clearing the path. Key takeaway: use the agent’s properties to tune motion and rely on SetDestination as the simple high-level command for navigation. How will you use stoppingDistance to control approach behavior in your game?

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.3 › NavMeshAgent: The Runtime Bridge
Core role

NavMeshAgent computes a path on the NavMesh and drives movement and steering to follow it while avoiding obstacles dynamically.

Important properties
  • speed — maximum movement speed.
  • acceleration — how quickly the agent reaches speed.
  • stoppingDistance — how close the agent gets before slowing.
  • autoBraking — whether the agent slows automatically on approach.
Example

During a chase, increase speed and keep stoppingDistance > 0 to avoid collision while maintaining pressure on the player.

Code call
// Example usage in a script
// agent.SetDestination(targetPosition);
// Check agent.remainingDistance and agent.pathPending to track progress
Remember: SetDestination initiates a path; the agent follows it subject to its movement properties. Use remainingDistance and isStopped to monitor and control behavior.

screens.title: PatrolAI: Patrol and Chase Logic
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough covers a practical PatrolAI pattern that alternates between patrolling random points and chasing a player when they come within range. The script starts by obtaining a NavMeshAgent reference in Start and sets default movement properties such as speed and stopping distance. Patrol logic selects a random point within a patrol radius and uses NavMesh. SamplePosition to ensure the point lies on the NavMesh; then it calls SetDestination. During Update, the script checks if the player is within chaseRange: if so, it switches to chase mode by increasing speed and calling SetDestination with the player's position. If the player leaves chaseRange, the script reverts to patrol settings and chooses another patrol point. A common misconception is assuming Random. insideUnitSphere yields a NavMesh point; it does not. Always sample the NavMesh to find a valid point before calling SetDestination. Another area to watch is agent. remainingDistance and agent. pathPending: use these to determine when a patrol destination is reached and when to pick the next point. Example runtime behavior: when the agent reaches a patrol point it chooses a new one, and when the player is nearby the agent chases and increases speed. Practice adjusting chaseRange, patrolRadius, and patrolInterval to tune responsiveness and variety. What value would you tune if the agent spends too long calculating paths? agent. pathPending diagnostics and simpler patrol intervals are useful starting points.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.3 › PatrolAI: Patrol and Chase Logic
Patrol pattern
// Structure shown for clarity
Start(): get NavMeshAgent, set speed and stoppingDistance, SetNewPatrolDestination();
Update(): if player in chaseRange -> agent.SetDestination(player.pos); else if reached patrol -> SetNewPatrolDestination();
SetNewPatrolDestination(): choose random point, use NavMesh.SamplePosition, agent.SetDestination(hit.position);
// Use remainingDistance and pathPending to validate reach
This code pattern separates concerns: sampling keeps patrols valid, agent properties tune motion, and the simple state switch controls behavior changes between patrol and chase.
Concrete example
Patrol radius 10, patrol interval 5 seconds, chase range 15. When player enters 15 units, agent speeds up and chases; when out of range, it resumes patrolling.
Misconception
Random points are not guaranteed valid NavMesh positions—always sample the NavMesh before setting a destination.
Key Takeaway

Use NavMesh.SamplePosition to ensure patrol points are valid and rely on agent properties to tune approach and chase behavior.

screens.title: Using NavMesh.SamplePosition
screens.narratorSegment: NavMesh. SamplePosition is a small but essential utility for creating valid patrol destinations. Random point generation often produces positions that fall off the NavMesh or inside obstacles. SamplePosition solves that by returning the closest valid NavMesh point within a search radius. Typical usage is to produce a random offset within a patrol radius and then call SamplePosition with that world position and a search radius equal or slightly larger than your patrol radius. If SamplePosition returns true, use the returned hit. position as the agent's destination; if it returns false, choose another random point or fall back to a safe default. For example, when building patrols around a patrolOrigin, pick a random direction and a random distance, add it to the origin, then call SamplePosition and check the outcome before calling SetDestination. A common pitfall is trusting SamplePosition with a search radius that is too small; it may fail to find a nearby NavMesh cell even if one exists slightly further away. Also avoid sampling on positions far above or below the expected height; sample near the ground plane. Closing question: how would you handle repeated SamplePosition failures to avoid an agent spinning in place? A good answer is to count attempts, increase search radius gradually, or temporarily stop the agent while you retry.

For example, when building patrols around a patrolOrigin, pick a random direction and a random distance, add it to the origin, then call SamplePosition and check the outcome before calling SetDestination. A common pitfall is trusting SamplePosition with a search radius that is too small; it may fail to find a nearby NavMesh cell even if one exists slightly further away. Also avoid sampling on positions far above or below the expected height; sample near the ground plane. Closing question: how would you handle repeated SamplePosition failures to avoid an agent spinning in place? A good answer is to count attempts, increase search radius gradually, or temporarily stop the agent while you retry.

keyIdea.title: Sample safely
keyIdea.text: Use NavMesh.SamplePosition to convert arbitrary world points into valid NavMesh destinations and handle failures gracefully.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.3 › Using NavMesh.SamplePosition
Sampling pattern
Vector3 randomPoint = origin + Random.insideUnitSphere * patrolRadius;
NavMeshHit hit;
if (NavMesh.SamplePosition(randomPoint, out hit, searchRadius, NavMesh.AllAreas)) {
    agent.SetDestination(hit.position);
} else {
    // fallback or retry
}
Make searchRadius equal or a bit larger than your patrolRadius to increase chance of finding a valid polygon. If sampling fails repeatedly, increase radius, count attempts, or pick a known safe point.
Concrete tip
Limit sampling attempts per frame to avoid CPU spikes. Retry over multiple frames or expand search radius on failure.
Misconception
Random points are valid by default. They are not; you must sample the NavMesh before using them as destinations.
Key Takeaway

Always validate random patrol points with NavMesh.SamplePosition and handle failure by retrying or falling back to safe patrol points.

screens.title: Tuning Runtime Properties
screens.narratorSegment: Runtime tuning gives your agents the feel you want: responsive patrols, believable chases, or ponderous bosses. Speed sets a hard top for movement, while acceleration controls how rapidly an agent reaches that speed. Angular speed sets how fast the agent rotates to face movement direction; low angular speed makes agents skid or take wide arcs. Stopping distance is critical for approach behavior—set it to the minimum comfortable gap between agent and target to prevent collisions or jitter. Auto Braking further controls whether the agent decelerates when nearing its destination; disabling it can create more continuous movement for certain behaviors. A concrete example: for a nimble scout you might set speed to 5, acceleration to 10, and angular speed high so it turns quickly. For a heavy guard, lower speed and acceleration, and higher stoppingDistance to keep it from crowding the player. Watch for these common mistakes: very high acceleration with low angular speed can cause unnatural sliding, and a stoppingDistance of zero may cause agents to attempt to overlap a target. When debugging movement, toggle autoBraking to observe approach behavior and inspect agent. remainingDistance to verify the agent recognizes the destination. What combination of these properties would you tune if your agent overshoots a patrol point repeatedly? Try lowering acceleration and enabling auto braking to smooth the approach.

screens.title: Common Baking and Navigation Issues
screens.narratorSegment: When agents get stuck or cannot reach an area, debugging usually falls into baking problems, object marking errors, or incorrect runtime settings. Start with visualization: inspect the NavMesh overlay in the Scene view and see if the walkable polygons cover the intended paths. If a corridor is missing, check Agent Radius and corridor width; a too-large radius will mark the corridor unwalkable. If ramps are excluded, increase Max Slope. If an agent reaches a destination but then does nothing, inspect agent. remainingDistance and agent. pathPending to see whether a path is still being computed or has been completed. Another common issue is collision between agents: tune Obstacle Avoidance Type or use NavMeshObstacle for dynamic blockers. Misconfigured Navigation Static flags can cause odd results—objects intended as obstacles must be set to Not Walkable. For runtime checks, use OnDrawGizmosSelected to visualize chaseRange, patrolRadius and the agent. path corners; this helps determine whether SetDestination is being set to a valid position and whether the path contains expected corners. A practical debugging approach: reproduce the stuck state, visualize the NavMesh, check agent properties, and then adjust bake parameters or object flags. If an agent has a valid path but seems not to move, ensure agent. isStopped is false and speed or acceleration are not zero. What will you check first when an agent reports a long remainingDistance but doesn't move? agent. pathPending and isStopped are good initial diagnostics.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn why a Navigation Mesh is the practical backbone for AI movement in 3D games and how Unity's NavMesh system helps agents find efficient, obstacle-aware routes. I will show you how baking converts scene geometry into a simplified map of walkable polygons, how agent parameters shape that map, and how the NavMeshAgent component turns high-level movement commands into smooth navigation at runtime. We will explore concrete steps you take in the Navigation window, how to mark objects for baking, and the essential runtime properties like speed, stopping distance, and obstacle avoidance. Along the way you'll practice a patrol-and-chase example that uses sampled NavMesh points so agents resume sensible behavior when a target is out of range. A common misconception is that AI movement must be handcrafted for every obstacle; baking and agents offload most of that complexity and give deterministic, efficient paths. By the end you should be able to bake a usable NavMesh, attach a NavMeshAgent, and debug why agents might get stuck. Think about an agent as a pedestrian: if you change the pedestrian's shoe size or stride, the map of passable sidewalks can change dramatically. How might that apply to different character sizes in your game?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why a NavMesh is used for efficient pathfinding, bake a NavMesh in the Unity editor, configure the agent parameters that shape walkable space, add a NavMeshAgent to a character and command it to move, and diagnose typical navigation issues. Specifically, you'll learn how Agent Radius, Height, Max Slope, and Step Height affect the baked result and how to mark objects correctly as navigation static. You'll practice driving an agent with SetDestination and creating patrol behavior by sampling valid NavMesh points. You'll also learn the runtime properties—speed, acceleration, stopping distance, and obstacle avoidance—which control motion and how agents approach targets. A common misconception is that baking is optional for intelligent avoidance; in practice, baking plus a properly configured agent is the most reliable path to responsive AI. These objectives map to practical milestones: successfully baking a NavMesh that covers intended areas, implementing a basic patrol AI, and resolving at least one navigation bug by inspecting paths and agent properties. Consider which objective you want to master first: baking accuracy or runtime tuning?

This second objectives screen focuses on practical skills and debugging steps you'll practice. You will configure agent properties and observe how they change the baked NavMesh, create patrol behavior with sampled NavMesh points, and implement chase logic so agents change speed and stopping distance during pursuit. We'll emphasize how to detect and fix baking mistakes like corridors becoming unwalkable because of an oversized agent radius, or slopes being rejected due to a low maximum slope setting. You'll run simple checks at runtime such as looking at agent. remainingDistance, checking agent. pathPending, and toggling isStopped to understand agent state. A helpful rule is to visualize the NavMesh after each baking iteration and test agents with the player or a test capsule. These hands-on habits will speed up debugging and make your AI feel reliable. Think about which runtime property you would test first if an agent overshoots its target: often stoppingDistance or auto-braking is the right place to start.

A NavMesh is a precomputed representation of the walkable areas in your scene, expressed as a connected network of polygons. This representation reduces complex geometry to a graph-like surface where each polygon is a region an agent can stand on and pathfinding algorithms compute shortest valid routes between points on that surface. The practical benefit is performance and reliability: path calculations run quickly because they operate on simplified polygons instead of raw mesh triangles, and agents avoid static obstacles automatically because the baking process excludes those areas. For example, imagine a game level with furniture, pillars, and ramps: the NavMesh will create a continuous set of navigable polygons over the floor and ramps while excluding the volume occupied by obstacles, so an enemy can compute a path around a table without per-frame collision checks. A common misconception is that NavMesh replaces physics-based avoidance; it does not. NavMesh handles static and baked geometry and gives agents passable routes, while dynamic obstacle avoidance and steering are still handled by the NavMeshAgent at runtime. Key takeaway: treat the NavMesh as the map of where agents may plan paths, and use agent settings to ensure that map matches your characters' footprint. How does your level geometry change when you imagine different agent sizes?

Baking transforms your scene into a NavMesh by scanning geometry and classifying surfaces as walkable or not. Start by opening the Navigation window and switching to the Bake tab. The key parameters there control how the NavMesh is generated: Agent Radius sets the minimum clearance around the agent footprint and influences which narrow passages remain walkable. Agent Height excludes low ceilings where an agent cannot fit. Max Slope limits how steep a surface may be to remain walkable, and Step Height defines the climbable step size. Drop Height and Jump Distance determine how much vertical movement or gaps an agent can traverse during baking. A concrete example: if you set Agent Radius to 0.5 meters and your doorway is 0.8 meters wide, that doorway will be considered passable. If you increase radius to 0.6, the doorway may become unwalkable and the NavMesh will not include it. Important debugging step: mark your ground as Navigation Static and obstacles as Not Walkable before baking; otherwise the NavMesh may include geometry you intend to block. After adjusting parameters, click Bake and inspect the blue overlay in the Scene view. If areas are missing, iteratively adjust parameters rather than assuming an agent bug. Which parameter would you change first if agents cannot climb a ramp? Max Slope is usually the answer.

The NavMesh only reflects objects you mark for inclusion in baking. In the Inspector, use the Navigation Static dropdown to mark ground and obstacles appropriately. Ground objects you want agents to walk on should be marked as Navigation Static and set to Walkable. Objects that should block navigation—walls, crates, and tall props—should be marked as Navigation Static but flagged Not Walkable, or handled as NavMeshObstacles when runtime movement is required. A common error is forgetting to mark an object as Navigation Static; the bake will then ignore it and agents might attempt to walk through it because it wasn't excluded. Another practical distinction is between static obstacles baked into the NavMesh and dynamic obstacles created at runtime with NavMeshObstacle; the former alters the baked polygons, the latter is resolved by the agent's avoidance system and local steering. For example, if you place a table and forget to mark it Not Walkable, the NavMesh will cover the table top area if it's flagged as walkable, creating a hole in behavior. Best practice: maintain a short checklist—mark ground walkable, mark level architecture as static, and treat moving platforms or doors as dynamic obstacles or update the NavMesh at runtime if necessary. Ask yourself: did I mark every major prop that should block movement as static before baking?

Agent parameters determine how baking interprets the environment and how agents behave at runtime. Agent Radius is the horizontal clearance the NavMesh assumes an agent needs; larger radii close narrow spaces during baking, while smaller radii can let agents squeeze through tight corridors. Agent Height matters for low ceilings and tunnels—if your character is tall but Agent Height is set low, you may bake walkable areas that real agents cannot occupy. Max Slope controls ramp traversability: set it too low and ramps will be excluded, too high and agents may attempt to climb surfaces you intended as walls. Step Height allows small vertical steps; if it's smaller than curb heights in your level, agents will treat those curbs as obstacles. Contrast two common scenarios: a nimble small enemy versus a large armored boss. You would bake the level with different Agent Radius and Height so both can navigate appropriate routes, or provide separate NavMesh areas per size. A common misconception is that a single NavMesh fits all agent sizes; in practice you may need multiple NavMesh layers or adjust baking for the primary agent type. Which property would you tune first if agents can’t traverse a ramp? Max Slope is the likely candidate, followed by visual confirmation in the Scene view.

The NavMeshAgent component is the runtime bridge between your gameplay logic and the precomputed NavMesh. It handles path calculation, steering, and local obstacle avoidance so your scripts can issue simple commands like SetDestination and rely on the agent to move sensibly. When you call SetDestination with a position on the NavMesh, the agent computes a path across polygons and begins moving, steering around static obstacles baked into the NavMesh and responding to dynamic obstacles based on its avoidance settings. For example, in a chase scenario you might increase agent. speed and leave stoppingDistance set to a value greater than zero so the agent approaches the player but does not collide. A frequent misconception is thinking SetDestination teleports or deterministically snaps an agent to the goal; instead it starts a calculated path and the agent follows it over time, subject to speed, acceleration and angular speed. Understanding NavMeshAgent state is important: agent. remainingDistance tells you how far remains on the current path, agent. pathPending indicates if path computation is ongoing, and agent. isStopped can pause movement without clearing the path. Key takeaway: use the agent’s properties to tune motion and rely on SetDestination as the simple high-level command for navigation. How will you use stoppingDistance to control approach behavior in your game?

This walkthrough covers a practical PatrolAI pattern that alternates between patrolling random points and chasing a player when they come within range. The script starts by obtaining a NavMeshAgent reference in Start and sets default movement properties such as speed and stopping distance. Patrol logic selects a random point within a patrol radius and uses NavMesh. SamplePosition to ensure the point lies on the NavMesh; then it calls SetDestination. During Update, the script checks if the player is within chaseRange: if so, it switches to chase mode by increasing speed and calling SetDestination with the player's position.
